newsitem.title: GERMANY: German cocoa grind unsurprising -- industry assn.
newsitem.headline: German cocoa grind unsurprising -- industry assn.

text.p: A lower German cocoa grind result in the first quarter of 1997 is the result of well-publicised capacity shifts within Europe, said Karsten Keunecke, managing director of German Confectionery Industry Association BDS.
"Capacity shifts have become part of the changed infrastructure -- more beans are ground in plants near sea ports and more semi-finished products are imported here," he said.
"Therefore the fall in the German result is not dramatic."
The figure dropped by 11.71 percent to 61,379.3 tonnes compared with 69,520.3 tonnes in the same 1996 period. But it exceeded the 56,254.7 tonnes seen in fourth quarter 1996.
Analysts last week forecast the first quarter data, the key pointer to chocolate demand, to be down at perhaps 60,000 tonnes, citing extremely high year-ago figures.
Keunecke confirmed early 1996 had been exceptionally high.
Early 1997 chocolate output figures had been positive, he added.
The Dutch result last Friday brought a slightly higher grind despite earlier expectations of a flat or slightly lower number, which also gave indication of good underlying demand.
With 102,338 tonnes of beans ground in the first quarter 1997, 1.46 percent up from last year, the Netherlands was the world's leading processor.
